security_hardening.title: Restrict CORS to trusted origins only
security_hardening.description: The Fastify adapter configures CORS with `origin: '*'` and `allowedHeaders: '*'`, allowing any domain to make cross-origin requests to the API. This is a critical misconfiguration for a multi-tenant municipal system handling sensitive citizen data including Norwegian national IDs (NIN), booking information, and GDPR-protected data.
security_hardening.rationale: Wildcard CORS allows malicious websites to make authenticated requests on behalf of logged-in users, potentially leading to data theft or unauthorized actions. In a government/municipal context handling PII, this violates GDPR requirements and Norwegian data protection regulations. The CORS_ORIGINS environment variable is already defined with production URLs but is not being used.
security_hardening.currentRisk: Any malicious website can make authenticated API requests when a user is logged in, stealing PII or performing unauthorized bookings
security_hardening.remediation: Replace wildcard CORS with an allowlist of trusted frontend domains. Use the existing `CORS_ORIGINS` environment variable: `origin: process.env.CORS_ORIGINS?.split(',') || ['http://localhost:5173', 'http://localhost:5174', 'http://localhost:5175']`. Also restrict `allowedHeaders` to specific required headers like 'Content-Type', 'Authorization', 'x-tenant-id', 'x-user-id'.

security_hardening.title: Replace predictable CSRF token generation with cryptographically secure tokens
security_hardening.description: The AuthController.getCsrf() method in auth.controller.ts generates CSRF tokens using `Buffer.from(Date.now().toString()).toString('base64')`, which produces completely predictable tokens that can be easily guessed by attackers. The token is just a base64-encoded timestamp with no cryptographic randomness.
security_hardening.rationale: CSRF tokens must be unpredictable to prevent cross-site request forgery attacks. A token derived from the current timestamp can be calculated by any attacker who knows the approximate request time (within seconds), completely defeating CSRF protection for state-changing operations like bookings and consent management.
security_hardening.vulnerability: CWE-330: Use of Insufficiently Random Values
security_hardening.currentRisk: Attackers can predict CSRF tokens and forge requests that appear to come from legitimate users, enabling unauthorized bookings or data modifications
security_hardening.remediation: Use Node.js crypto module to generate cryptographically secure random tokens: `import crypto from 'crypto'; const csrfToken = crypto.randomBytes(32).toString('hex');`. Consider using @fastify/csrf-protection plugin for production-grade CSRF handling with token binding to sessions.

security_hardening.title: Implement password verification in email/password login endpoint
security_hardening.description: The login endpoint at POST /api/auth/login in auth.controller.ts finds users by email but does not verify passwords. Lines 29-42 query the user by email, and if found, immediately generate a JWT token without any password validation. The function claims to be 'Email/password login' but only checks the email exists.
security_hardening.rationale: Email addresses are often publicly known or easily guessable, especially for municipality staff (firstname.lastname@kommune.no pattern). Without password verification, the entire authentication system is bypassed, giving attackers full access to any user account including admin roles.
security_hardening.vulnerability: CWE-306: Missing Authentication for Critical Function
security_hardening.currentRisk: Anyone can log in as any user (including admin accounts) by simply knowing or guessing their email address. No credential validation occurs.
security_hardening.remediation: 1) Add password_hash column to users table using bcrypt/argon2. 2) Require password in login request body with Zod validation. 3) Compare hashed passwords before issuing JWT: `const isValid = await bcrypt.compare(body.password, user.passwordHash); if (!isValid) return 401;`. 4) Return generic 'Invalid credentials' error for both wrong email and wrong password to prevent user enumeration.

security_hardening.title: Disable GraphiQL playground in production environment
security_hardening.description: The API registers the GraphQL endpoint in main.ts with `graphiql: true`, enabling the interactive GraphQL playground in all environments including production. This exposes the complete API schema, allows arbitrary query execution, and provides introspection capabilities to potential attackers.
security_hardening.rationale: GraphiQL in production exposes internal API structure for reconnaissance. Attackers can discover undocumented queries, understand data relationships, and craft complex nested queries that could cause denial of service. For a government platform handling sensitive municipal data, API introspection should be disabled in production.
security_hardening.currentRisk: Attackers can explore the full GraphQL schema, discover all available queries/mutations, understand data models, and potentially craft expensive nested queries to overload the server
security_hardening.remediation: Conditionally enable GraphiQL only in development: `graphiql: process.env.NODE_ENV !== 'production'`. Also add query complexity limits and depth limiting using mercurius validation: `validationRules: [depthLimit(10), queryComplexity({ maximumComplexity: 1000 })]`.

security_hardening.title: Remove sensitive PII from ID-porten authentication debug logging
security_hardening.description: The ID-porten authentication controller (idporten.controller.ts) contains 40+ console.log statements that output highly sensitive data including Norwegian National Identity Numbers (NIN/fødselsnummer), full session data objects, cookie contents, JWT tokens, and user details. These are production console statements, not conditionally disabled.
security_hardening.rationale: Norwegian NIN is among the most sensitive PII under GDPR and Norwegian personal data regulations. The logs include statements like `console.log('Full session data:', JSON.stringify(sessionData))` and `console.log('Extracted NIN:', nin)`. This data in logs creates compliance violations, breach liability, and potential vectors for identity theft.
security_hardening.vulnerability: CWE-532: Insertion of Sensitive Information into Log File
security_hardening.currentRisk: Norwegian national IDs, session tokens, and authentication data are written to production logs, violating GDPR Article 32 (security of processing) and creating significant breach liability under Norwegian data protection law
security_hardening.remediation: 1) Replace all console.log with the existing pino logger that has field redaction configured for 'ssn', 'cookie', 'token'. 2) Remove NIN logging entirely or mask to first 6 digits pattern. 3) Wrap debug-level logs in environment check: `if (process.env.LOG_LEVEL === 'debug')`. 4) Never log full session objects - extract only safe identifiers for tracing.

alreadyPlannedItems: Rate limiting on authentication endpoints (NOW IMPLEMENTED in rate-limit.middleware.ts)
metadata.notesOnAnalysis: This updated security audit identified NEW vulnerabilities not covered by existing planned features. Key findings: CORS wildcard misconfiguration despite CORS_ORIGINS being defined, predictable CSRF tokens using Date.now(), missing password verification in login flow, GraphiQL enabled in production, and extensive PII logging in auth flows. Rate limiting was previously flagged but has since been implemented with proper auth endpoint protection.
